passages.t: ‘Let the redeemed of the LORD say so’: the lost and the prisoners
passages.happening:
Psalm 107 opens Book Five, the last of the five books of the Psalms. It begins with a call to thank God. “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 1). Then comes a summons: “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy” (verse 2). These are people God has gathered “from east and west, from north and south” (verse 3).

Then the psalm tells four stories of rescue. The first two come here.

The first is about travellers lost in the desert. “Some wandered in desert wastelands, finding no path to a city in which to dwell” (verse 4). They are hungry and thirsty and close to fainting (verse 5). “Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress” (verse 6). He leads them straight to a city where they can live (verse 7).

The second is about prisoners. “Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains” (verse 10). This time the psalm says why they were there. They had rebelled against God's words (verse 11). They fall and no one helps (verse 12). Then they cry out, and he saves them. “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains” (verse 14).

After each rescue the same line returns. “Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men” (verses 8 and 15).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 106, the last psalm of Book Four, ended with a prayer: “gather us from the nations” (Psalm 106:47). Psalm 107 begins with people who have been gathered from the lands (verse 3). Whoever arranged the book set an answer right after the prayer. Many scholars think the psalm, or at least its opening, comes from after the return from exile in Babylon. The book page's part on when the psalms were written tells that story.

To be ‘redeemed’ was to be bought back or set free by someone with the right and the power to do it. A family member could redeem a relative sold into debt. Here God himself is the one who buys his people back.

Notice the shape of each story. Trouble. A cry to the LORD. Rescue. Thanks. The same two refrains come four times in the psalm: ‘Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble’ (verses 6, 13, 19 and 28) and ‘Let them give thanks’ (verses 8, 15, 21 and 31). A first hearer would soon be singing along.

The two kinds of trouble are different. The travellers in the desert did nothing wrong; they were simply lost. The prisoners brought their trouble on themselves. Yet the same cry is heard, and the same God answers. ‘Gates of bronze’ and ‘bars of iron’ (verse 16) were the defences of a strong city. Only a great power could break them.
passages.later:
God promised through Isaiah, “I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west” (Isaiah 43:5). Psalm 107 sings as if that has begun.

Mary sang words very close to verse 9 when she was carrying Jesus: “He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53). And Jesus began his work in Nazareth by reading a prophecy about freedom: “He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18).
passages.asks:
The psalm says, ‘Let the redeemed of the LORD say so.’ Thanks is meant to be spoken out loud, not only felt.

Which story is yours? Some people are lost without knowing how they got there. Some are stuck in a prison they built themselves. Psalm 107 says that both may cry out, and both have been heard. If you have been rescued, say so. Someone else may need to hear it.

passages.t: The sick and the sailors: ‘He calmed the storm to a whisper’
passages.happening:
The third story is about people near death from sickness. “Fools, in their rebellious ways, and through their iniquities, suffered affliction” (verse 17). They cannot eat and come close to “the gates of death” (verse 18). They cry out, and he saves them. “He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit” (verse 20). The refrain follows, and then a call to bring thank offerings (verses 21 and 22).

The fourth story is the longest. “Others went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters” (verse 23). God raises a storm (verse 25). The ship climbs to the sky and drops into the deep, and the sailors lose their nerve (verse 26). “They reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their skill was useless” (verse 27).

They cry out, and he answers. “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (verse 29). They are glad of the quiet, and he guides them “to the harbor they desired” (verse 30). The refrain comes one last time, with a call to praise God before the whole people and their elders (verses 31 and 32).
passages.hearers:
Israel was not a nation of sailors. In its poems the sea was often a picture of chaos and danger, a power only God could tame. A hearer in the hills of Judah would feel the terror of verse 26 even if he had never seen a ship. Notice that the psalm says the sailors saw God's “wonders in the deep” (verse 24). The storm itself showed them who rules the sea.

In verse 17 the sickness comes after foolish and rebellious living. The psalm is telling one kind of story here, not every story. Other parts of the Bible, such as the book of Job, refuse to say that all sickness is a punishment.

Verse 20 is striking. God heals by sending his word, the way a king sends a messenger with an order. A word from him is enough.

A ‘sacrifice of thanksgiving’ (verse 22) was an offering brought to the temple after a rescue. The person who brought it often told the story aloud to those gathered there.
passages.later:
Jonah's ship nearly broke up when “the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea” (Jonah 1:4).

The Gospels tell of a night when Jesus was asleep in a boat in a storm. He got up and spoke to the wind and the waves, and “the wind died down, and it was perfectly calm” (Mark 4:39). The disciples asked, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41). A hearer who knew Psalm 107 knew whose work that was.

A Roman officer once asked Jesus to heal his servant from a distance: “just say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8). He believed what verse 20 says.
passages.hard:
All four stories in Psalm 107 end with a rescue. Many people have cried out and were not rescued in the way they hoped. The psalm is a song of thanks sung by people who were brought through. It is not a promise that every prayer is answered the same way. The same book keeps Psalm 88, which never turns. If your storm has not calmed, the note on Psalm 88 is for you, and so is Find Help.

Verse 17 does not mean that every sick person is to blame. The psalm tells one story of people who were. Do not use it to judge anyone who is ill, including yourself.
passages.asks:
The sailors' skill was ‘useless’, and that is when they cried out. Many people only pray when their own strength runs out. The psalm does not scorn them for it. God heard them anyway.

Is there a storm in your life now? You may tell God about it plainly. If he has brought you into a quiet harbour before, tell someone that story. That is what the psalm means by praising him ‘in the assembly of the people’.

passages.t: God turns the land around: ‘Let him who is wise pay heed’
passages.happening:
The last part of the psalm changes its form. There are no more stories with refrains. Instead it describes how God turns things upside down.

He can turn rivers into desert, and good land into salt flats, “because of the wickedness of its dwellers” (verses 33 and 34). He can also do the reverse. “He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs” (verse 35). He brings the hungry there to build a city (verse 36). They sow fields and plant vineyards, and he blesses them (verses 37 and 38).

When people are crushed by oppression, he acts again (verse 39). “He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland” (verse 40). “But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks” (verse 41). The upright see it and are glad, and wickedness is silenced (verse 42).

The psalm ends like a teacher. “Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
This part sounds like the book of Proverbs. It is wisdom: a way of looking at the world and seeing God's hand in its changes.

Notice the reversals. The proud nobles end up wandering in a wasteland with no path (verse 40). That is exactly where the lost travellers were at the start of the psalm (verse 4). The hungry end up in a city (verse 36), which is what the travellers were looking for. God brings down the strong and raises the weak.

‘Fields of salt’ (verse 34) were land that could grow nothing. ‘Pools of water’ in the desert (verse 35) was a picture the prophets used for God bringing his people home.

The last verse is an invitation to think, not just to feel. The wise person looks back over these stories and sees one thread running through them: the loving devotion of the LORD, his hesed. The book page explains that word.
passages.later:
Hannah sang the same truth long before: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8). Psalm 113 will sing it again soon after.

Jesus told of a son who wandered far from home and came back. His father said, “He was lost and is found!” (Luke 15:24). The lost traveller of Psalm 107 has a long family in Scripture.
passages.asks:
The psalm ends with homework. Look back over your own life. Where has God brought you out of a desert, or a dark place, or a storm? Where has he humbled you, or lifted you up?

Wisdom, in Psalm 107, is not knowing many facts. It is noticing God's loving devotion in the turns of a life. That takes time and slow attention. The psalm asks you to give it both.
